title: Spinach and Agushi Curry
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: The stew's colour changes from pink to mustard as it cooks — the clearest visual endpoint in the collection.
longDesc: Melon seed and spinach in a chalé sauce base, and it has two of the best cues in the whole Ghanaian record. The chalé sauce simmers twenty minutes on low, then a hundred grams of agushi goes in and the sauce should turn creamy. Crushed guinea peppers and lime juice follow for ten minutes, and the stew colour changes from pink to mustard — a visual endpoint you cannot mistake. Finally the spinach goes in and you simmer gently until it wilts. Grilled plantain, twelve to fifteen minutes turning halfway, is the optional accompaniment.
ingredients: 100 g (about 2 heaped tbsp) agushi — dried ground melon seeds
150-300 ml water or vegetable stock, if required
Melted coconut oil and olive oil, for drizzling
equipment: Grill or griddle, for the plantain
steps: Heat the coconut oil and soften the onion.
Add the curry powder and chilli powder.
Add the chalé sauce and simmer over low heat 20 minutes.
Stir in the agushi — the sauce should turn creamy.
Add the crushed guinea peppers and the lime juice and simmer 10 minutes.
The stew colour changes from pink to mustard.
Add water or stock if required.
Add the spinach and simmer gently until it wilts.
Season with salt and black pepper.
For the plantain: season with ginger, chilli flakes and salt, drizzle with oil, and grill 12 to 15 minutes, turning halfway.
chefTips: Pink to mustard is the cue and it is the clearest visual endpoint in this collection. Before the colour shifts the melon seed has not cooked out.
The sauce should turn creamy as the agushi goes in. Two cues in sequence, and both are worth waiting for.
A hundred grams of agushi is given as about two heaped tablespoons, which is a useful conversion for a dense powder.
Water or stock only if required, and the range is wide — a hundred and fifty to three hundred millilitres. Judge by thickness.
Guinea peppers crushed, eight of them, and they are optional. They are grains of paradise and they lift the whole dish.
Spinach in at the very end, simmered gently just until it wilts. Baby leaf is specified and it needs almost nothing.
Vegan as written, which is unusual for an agushi dish — most Ghanaian melon-seed stews lean on fish or meat.
commonMistakes: Serving before the colour turns from pink to mustard.
Adding all the water at once.
Boiling the spinach rather than wilting it.
Using cooked chalé sauce where uncooked is specified.
Skipping the lime juice, which brightens the melon seed.
sources: Adapted from 'Spinach and Agushi Curry (with grilled plantain)' by Zoe Adjonyoh, published on stylist.co.uk, 5 February 2021. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'By Stylist Team'; the page credits the recipes to Adjonyoh. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS). Yield as printed: 'Serves: 4–6'.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 tbsp coconut oil; 1 small onion, thinly sliced; 2 tsp curry powder; 1 tsp chilli powder; 350ml uncooked chalé sauce; 100g (about 2 heaped tbsp) agushi (dried ground melon seeds); 8 guinea peppers, crushed (optional); juice of 1 lime; 150–300ml water or vegetable stock, if required; 200g baby leaf spinach; 1 tsp sea salt; 1 tsp coarsely ground black pepper. Grilled plantain, optional: 4–6 ripe plantains; 1 tbsp ground ginger; ½ tbsp dried chilli flakes; sea salt; coconut oil (melted) and olive oil, for drizzling.
A CONVERSION WORTH NOTING: '100g (about 2 heaped tbsp)' of agushi. Two heaped tablespoons weighing a hundred grams is plausible for a dense ground seed and is reproduced as printed.

THE CUES, all three quoted and in sequence: chalé sauce simmered 'over low heat 20 minutes'; then with the agushi, 'sauce should turn creamy'; then after the guinea peppers and lime, 'Stew colour changes from pink to mustard.' Then the spinach: 'simmer gently until spinach wilts'. THE PINK-TO-MUSTARD CUE IS THE SINGLE CLEAREST VISUAL ENDPOINT in the Ghanaian material consulted.
Plantain as printed: grill '12–15 minutes, turning halfway through'.
IT DEPENDS ON uncooked chalé sauce, published at GHA031 with its divergent later printing at GHA032. Note the recipe specifies UNCOOKED, so the raw blended base rather than the cooked sauce.

ON AGUSHI: dried ground melon seeds, the same ingredient as the agushi that clumps in kontomire stew (GHA023) and binds palaver sauce (GHA024). Here it is used as a creamy thickener rather than for clumps, which is a different treatment of the same seed.

ON GUINEA PEPPERS: Aframomum melegueta, grains of paradise, the same spice she calls 'guinea peppers' in her shito (GHA051) and 'grains of paradise' in her grilled tilapia (GHA095). Three names for one spice across one author's recipes.
VEGAN AS WRITTEN, which distinguishes it from every other documented Ghanaian melon-seed dish — the traditional versions all carry fish, meat or both.
storage: 4 days refrigerated, 3 months frozen. Add fresh spinach on reheating.
reheating: Gentle heat with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Melon seeds are high in plant protein, magnesium, zinc and healthy fats.
Spinach contributes iron, folate, vitamin K and vitamin A.
Vegan and a complete protein when served with rice.
Lime juice improves the absorption of the spinach's iron.
culturalNote: Agushi stews are everywhere in Ghana and almost always carry fish or meat, so a vegan version built on melon seed alone is a genuine diaspora contribution rather than a compromise. The pink-to-mustard colour change is the kind of cue that someone only writes down after watching the pot carefully more than once.
